summary:
Illinois stands under the national framework of the United States, where travel documents remain the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed federal agencies to use "sex" rather than "gender."

The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are adjudicated only as M or F from supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed the restriction to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992, and the ACLU is suing on behalf of seven plaintiffs. By March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports being confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening carries its own exposure. The State Department announced on 25 February 2025 that it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth. Separately, Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

Against this federal backdrop, Illinois is among the more protective states for a trans visitor already inside its borders. A July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills places Illinois in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier, whose laws have "gone above and beyond in safeguarding" trans rights.

Illinois bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, credit and public accommodations, in force since 1 June 2006, with "sexual orientation" defined to include gender-related identity whether or not traditionally associated with designated sex at birth. Hate-crime penalties were expanded to cover gender identity by HB 3930, signed 20 July 2015 and effective 1 January 2016, after prior coverage only as perceived sexual orientation. The gay and trans panic defense was repealed by SB 1761, signed 25 August 2017 and effective 1 January 2018.

Illinois holds a shield or refuge law protecting patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care legal in Illinois was banned in the patient's home state, a provision directly relevant to visitors travelling from ban states. Gender-affirming care legislation was signed 13 January 2023 and took effect immediately, covering care within Illinois including for individuals coming from outside the state to seek services. Illinois Medicaid covers reassignment surgery costs for applicants aged at least 21, and in June 2024 the Department of Human Services and the Public Health Institute of Metropolitan Chicago announced expansion through the Transgender and Gender Diverse Wellness and Equity Program.

Identity documents are comparatively open. Birth-certificate gender-marker change no longer requires operation after legislation passed 31 May 2017 and signed 25 August 2017, effective 1 January 2018, requiring an Affidavit and Certificate of Correction Request plus a Declaration of Gender Transition or Intersex Condition by a licensed health or mental health professional and a $15 fee. An X option has been available since July 2020, self-attestation reform passed in early 2023 took effect 1 July, and since 1 July 2024 persons born outside Illinois can change sex on an Illinois birth certificate. Driver's licence and state ID correction proceeds on a Gender Designation Change Form, with X available from 2024.

Facilities rules are permissive. Single-occupancy public restrooms were designated gender-neutral by legislation passed in 2019 and effective 1 January 2020. Chicago's Human Rights Ordinance, as amended in 2016, provides that each person determines their own gender identity with no proof required except expression for bathroom access, and all Chicago public schools have all-gender bathrooms by signage since December 2021. A May 2023 multi-occupancy permissive-use bill passed both houses but awaited the governor's signature or veto.

Transgender students are protected by a 30 June 2019 executive order establishing a task force and procedures for names, pronouns and dress codes, and the state's anti-bullying law requires school investigation, student privacy protection and staff training on bullying based on gender identity or expression. Conversion therapy on minors under 18 by mental health providers was banned under the Youth Mental Health Protection Act, signed 20 August 2015 and effective 1 January 2016.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 June 2014, gender-neutral marriage certificates have been available under a July 2021 law, and out-of-jurisdiction null-and-void provisions were repealed effective 2024. Civil unions have been recognised since 1 June 2011. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1 January 1962, when Illinois became the first state to eliminate sodomy laws.
tangentialFactors:
Illinois sits inside a national environment that is moving in the opposite direction to its own statutes. Federal measures in force or in litigation include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.

The federal posture on care and custody is hostile. Executive Order 14187 of 28 January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as mutilation, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19, including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and in October 2025 proposed health-department rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

Nationally, 16 states and the District of Columbia, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, hold healthcare shield laws, while 32 states and 5 territories, covering 56%, hold none. Illinois is on the shielding side of that split, which matters for a visitor travelling from a ban state.

Facilities exposure varies sharply across the United States. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and, in some states, government buildings cover 9 states and 1 territory, and some states make trans use of facilities a criminal offence in certain circumstances; 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. In April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol after declaring an intention to break the law; civil-rights attorneys described it as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Identity documents are also being closed elsewhere. In March 2026 Kansas enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities, which rights groups call a template for other state legislatures. Equality-map research shows the conditions for changing a gender marker on a licence or birth certificate differ state by state.

Official hostility extends to enforcement machinery. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called radical gender ideology, describing such activists as domestic terrorist groups. A May 2026 national counterterrorism strategy stated that counterterrorism activity would prioritise the rapid identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is described as anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist.

Custody is a documented site of harm nationally. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies for transgender inmates that mandate cutting their hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and psychiatric drugs; the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men were subjected to forced-labour programmes with guards justifying them by saying they would treat them "like a man," and those who refused faced beatings and solitary confinement; severe sexual abuse was also widely reported.

outOfScopeNotes:
A May 2023 multi-occupancy permissive-use restroom bill passed both houses of the Illinois legislature but the sources do not record whether the governor signed or vetoed it; the operative status is unresolved.

The July 2026 national legal-risk ranking is a rubric-based assessment by a single research project rather than a court or agency finding; its "Most Protective" tier placement is not independently corroborated in the sources.

The scope of Illinois's shield law as applied to a non-resident visitor, as distinct to a resident travelling from a ban state, is not spelled out in the sources; the law's text on out-of-state patients is not quoted.

Whether Illinois's hate-crime and non-discrimination provisions have been tested against the federal redefinition of sex under Executive Order 14168 is not sourced; state and federal definitions may diverge in practice without a recorded case.

The status of the ACLU's challenge to the passport sex-marker restrictions, and of the several federal executive orders blocked or enjoined in court, changes over time; the sources do not fix a current position on each measure.
